**Verdict:** Yes. He'd have you admit your flaws in the ad itself, and he calls it possibly his favorite tactic. Pick the real complaints about your product, state each one plainly, then follow with "but" and the claim you want believed. Add humor if you can.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high)

**Why he'd say it**
- Trust matters more to him than the size of the promise: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 13:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s).
- He prefers the trade: "I would rather always sacrifice promise to gain trust" (same source, @ 13:09).
- He says to admit flaws as a matter of course: "you want to always own your flaws of course you have them of course your product isn't perfect say so" (@ 12:30).
- On the 12:30 timestamp, he says "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions".

**How to word it**
1. **Collect the flaws.** He says to "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" (@ 15:03). Use what customers already complain about, so the ad answers the objections they already have. He frames it as: "we want to address all of the concerns they have upfront in our damaging admissions" (@ 13:44).
2. **Put the flaw first and the strength after "but".** "The statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" (@ 13:44). His example is "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" (@ 15:03). So the pattern is: *[true, damaging thing], but [the result you want believed]*.
3. **Keep it light.** "If you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" (@ 15:39).
4. **Say the true thing others won't.** "If you want to stand out in a crowded marketplace tell the truth" (@ 15:39), and "what people won't say is the truth" (@ 16:15).

**Where it goes**
- The same idea applies on sales calls. For an offer that sounds too good to be true, he front-loads the downsides: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad." ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 19:42, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s). The point of doing this is "So then they can self-qualify." (@ 20:14).
- This pairs with his advice to say who the ad isn't for. He calls that "even more powerful than the original call out" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 5:02). A flaw that rules out the wrong buyer ("not for you if you need X") does both jobs.

**What they've done:** He says his websites are ugly but convert ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:03). The vault doesn't show him running a specific flaw-admitting ad, so that example is his own illustration of the pattern.

**What would change their answer:** The vault has no case where he says to skip admissions. The limits come from his own rule. The flaw has to be true and something prospects actually complain about. The claim after "but" has to be real, because the sentence only works if what follows the "but" is believed. A flaw that is the buyer's main reason to say no is a different case. The vault doesn't cover it, so I'd treat it as untested.

**Caveat on his evidence:** He backs this with unnamed research and an Eminem rap-battle story. Both are illustrations, not his own data ([[marketing/copywriting/damaging-admissions]]).

**Verdict:** Aim for under 10% monthly churn, which he calls best-in-class. About 20% (80% retention) is typical for a paid community. Start worrying when churn is above 30%, meaning fewer than 7 in 10 members stay month to month. At that point he says retention is the highest-ROI thing you can work on. Before you judge any of these numbers, split your members by how long they've been with you.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). The benchmarks are Skool platform averages from one video, so it's a single source.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Worry threshold:** "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s)
- **Why it's worth fixing:** halving churn doubles lifetime value. "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" (@ 2:13).
- **Churn depends on tenure.** "the biggest rule is that churn drops dramatically with time" (@ 3:19).
  - "if you keep someone 90 days, which seems to be the first kind of big churn drop-off point, it drops to around 10% or less" (@ 3:53).
  - "by month six, so another 90 days after that, churn gets extremely low. So, it goes from like 10% to 2%." (@ 3:53)
- **How to read your number:** he says to ask "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" instead of "How do I make this number go down?" (@ 4:24). He admits he has obsessed over the average himself.
- **Don't overreact:** "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks" (@ 4:24). Month one is the biggest churn month, so have "a very specific strategy for getting people past the first month" (@ 4:57).
- **What fixes it at each stage:** by day 90 they need "some sort of outcome, some sort of change in behavior." By month six it's "them connecting with other people within that community" (@ 5:31).
- **Simple tracking:** track joins against cancels each month and label the business growing, flat or declining (@ 0:33). Growth "looks like a flat retention curve, and then what happens is it just keeps growing" (@ 19:11).

**What he'd have you do about it** (from [[business/retention/community-and-belonging]] and [[business/retention/overwhelm-and-onboarding]])
- Show up in the community daily. He says owners who did had "significantly higher retention" (@ 13:39).
- Get each member one real friend, and introduce newcomers to about ten regulars.
- Cut scope, because overwhelm is the number one churn driver after price.
- Offer annual plans, since "annual always has lower churn than monthly" (@ 15:52).

**What would change his answer**
- **Community age:** if your community is under 90 days or six months old, the average will look inflated. The older members who churn least aren't in the data yet, so don't panic.
- **Business type:** he says the benchmarks fit online and consumer services, not things like insurance or alarm systems.
- **Source limits:** the numbers are Skool averages that he attributes to Skool's founder, and he's involved with Skool.

**Verdict:** Pay off the $60k, and do it fast, over about 4–5 months, while you keep growing with the cash flow the business already generates. Hormozi says he skews "very close to the Ramsey side" on business debt.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). In a 2026-05 consult he coached an HVAC-duct cleaner with $60,000 of business debt, and that's close to your exact situation.

**Why he'd say it**
- He treats it as safety plus peace of mind more than as a financial optimization: "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)
- "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37)
- His one argument is that debt adds risk that comes due: "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10) and "businesses have seasons, they have volatility" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10).
- He points to enduring companies that run debt-free: "a lot of like Chick-fil-A operate debt free." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10)
- It fits his general rule of safety first so you can take risk later: "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible. Like do whatever you got to do to get your oxygen mask on." ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 17:53)

**What he's done:** In that consult he put "continue to pay off the debt" second on the client's priority list, right after a 10% price increase ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45). Debt payoff wasn't an alternative to growth. It ran alongside price, funnel and ad fixes.

**It isn't either/or.** He'd have you fund growth from the cheap, proven levers while the debt gets paid:
1. Raise prices. If you close 80% or more, "there's room" to charge more, and a raise pays off as long as you still close more than 65% ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06).
2. Fix the funnel and ad creative on what already works.
3. Raise ad spend only while returns hold: "we just want to continue to spend month over month provided our ROAS and our CAC stay more or less the same." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 10:48)

The price increase is what pays the debt down faster. You aren't choosing between the two.

**What would change his answer**
- He asked the client why the debt was taken on ("cuz I wanted to grow faster"), but the vault never says when borrowing to grow is justified. So I can't tell you he'd refuse debt-funded growth in every case. His own account is that he does endorse taking "greater and greater risk" on proven ad returns ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 11:54).
- His view on leverage is inconsistent. A month later he described heavy debt as how fund managers get rich ([[yt-sL16tsGafcQ]] @ 18:02), and he never reconciles that with his Ramsey lean. See [[tensions]].
- The vault doesn't say what he'd do with very cheap debt or with a growth channel returning far more than the interest. My read is that he'd still pay it off, but that's a guess.

**My own note:** He calls this "more of an emotional thing", so it's a preference, not a calculation. The vault gives no numbers on your interest rate or payback period. If your rate is low and you have a channel with a proven, fast payback, the math may favor keeping the cash. You'd be going against his instinct there.

**Verdict:** No, don't hold prices to protect the close rate. Hormozi would read an 82% close rate as a sign you're underpriced, and he'd raise prices about 10%. He would keep the raise only if you still close above roughly 65%.

**Based on:** said it. This is close to your exact case. The vault has him telling an HVAC-cleaning owner this in a consult.

**Why he'd say it**
- He treats a high close rate as a symptom, not something to protect: "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
- He gives a break-even test: "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." (same source @ 8:06)
- He says a higher price often doesn't hurt closing, because it makes the customer more sure you'll deliver: "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." (@ 7:00)
- He says underpricing costs you sales: "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (@ 7:33)
- For owners under about $3–5M in revenue, he calls charging more "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business" (@ 8:06). You're at $1.2M.

**What he's done:** In the same consult, his team had earlier told an HVAC-cleaning owner his business was mispriced for its space. The owner raised prices 23% and closed more (@ 6:26). Alex then proposed another 10% (to about $1,650 per unit). He penciled that out as roughly a 25% increase in net profit at the previous year's volume.

**Your numbers (my arithmetic, not his):** Assume your cost to do a job stays the same, so the extra price is all profit. A 10% raise then lifts profit per job from about 38% of the old price to about 48%. You'd break even on total profit at roughly a 65% close rate (0.82 × 0.38 / 0.48 ≈ 0.65). That matches his rule of thumb. The extra margin is large, so you could lose a lot of closes and still come out ahead. If your 38% includes fixed overhead, the real margin on each added dollar is even higher.

**What would change his answer:**
- You're capacity-constrained or have a supply problem. He opens every consult by asking whether the business is supply- or demand-constrained ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 3:47). That changes what the price is for, though a capacity limit usually argues for raising price too.
- You sell as a luxury or status product. He says his claim is about trust in delivery, not Veblen goods.
- Your close rate drops below the break-even point after the raise. He frames the 10% as "more asking than telling" and conditional on that. So test it and measure.

**How to run it (his approach, applied to you):** Raise about 10%, track the close rate for a few weeks, and keep going if it stays above about 65%. He also says to ignore "too expensive" complaints from people who aren't your ideal customer ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 8:46). Don't read those as proof you went too far.

**Caveat:** He's a single voice here, and the 65% rule and the HVAC story come from one 2026-05 consult. The caveat that matters is that his 80% threshold is a heuristic, not a measurement of your market. His own tests are the only check on it.

Quick status: I've found the passage in the raw transcript, and the premise looks wrong. The story isn't Hormozi's.

**Correction:** Hormozi doesn't tell this story. The host, Steven Bartlett, tells it on *The Diary of a CEO* (E235, 2023-04-03, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s)). Hormozi is the guest. The wiki has no page on it, so it's only in the raw transcript, and Bartlett isn't a vault member. I'm relaying it as Bartlett's account, not as Hormozi's view. This is the "reported" case, so it doesn't count as Hormozi's own statement.

**Bartlett's story**

- **The 4x valuation.** He says his company went public on a European exchange. On the road show, an investment bank told him the business would be worth more on a different market: "if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more which meant that my net worth would be Forex just by taking the exact same business and moving it to a different Stock Exchange" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:12).
- **The lesson he drew.** He later asked where his skill set was most valuable. He could help a local gym for about $1,000, or he could help a company heading into an IPO, where a good story can swing the valuation by "hundreds of millions" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:35:17).
- **The equity deal.** He took the IPO route and was paid in equity. His account: "the equity that I got for for the 9 to 12 months work that i' done was worth in the region of 7 to8 million," which he calls "basically freelance" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:35:51). Per the same passage, the first IPO company listed at about $3 billion.
- **What came next.** He started his own agency, which he names as Flight Story, with about 100 people after a year and a half. It began in the IPO market, then added biotech and other areas ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:36:23).

**Hormozi's only link to it** is a passing reference later in the episode. While talking about capital as a type of leverage, he says "you saw like the IPO money like the fact that the NASDAQ was Forex" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:45:47). He uses Bartlett's story as an example of public-market capital being far larger than friends-and-family or institutional money. That is the extent of his own use of it.

**Based on:** a quote from the raw transcript, with the story belonging to Bartlett. The wiki doesn't cover it.

**Caveat:** the transcript is auto-captioned, so the figures and names may be transcribed imprecisely (for example "dorf exchange" for what's probably Frankfurt).

**Verdict:** The vault doesn't support your premise. Hormozi told that roofing owner the opposite: stay on door-knocking and go all in on it.

**Based on:** said it. This is from the roofing-owner source, [[yt-o64cI6tebnU]]. I searched all four raw sources that mention roofing and found no mention of Google Ads in any of them.

**What he actually told him**
- "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." (@ 9:49)
- "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." (@ 10:54). "DDD" is the auto-caption for "D2D", door-to-door.
- At 24:27 the recap says: "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine."

**Why he said it**
- His rule is to put everything behind the highest-return channel you can run right now: "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." (@ 3:16)
- This owner could already close about 1 sale per 20 doors, and Hormozi treats that reliability as rare. "knowing how to go get money is one of the ways to do that." (@ 3:49)
- He said not to get clever with new channels: "Like I don't think we need to be cute about this." (@ 10:21) The scaling move was to hire reps paid per door knocked. That was his illustration: roughly $10 a door, from a 10% commission on a hoped-for $4K ticket across about 50 doors per sale.

The same source also covers a 90-day follow-up. The owner reported going from a little under $32K to about $247K in revenue. That figure is his own, and the vault doesn't say whether it's monthly or cumulative.

**What would change the answer:** I can't tell you what would flip his advice from the vault, because he never discussed Google Ads for this owner. If you saw that advice somewhere, it may be a different video or a different guest. Tell me which one and I'll check whether it's in the vault. The vault's advertising pages are at `wiki/marketing/advertising/_overview.md`.
